summary: Street photography is a genre of photography that captures unposed, candid moments in public places, often emphasizing decisive moments and human character. It has roots in 19th-century precursors and evolved through the 20th century with influential practitioners like Henri Cartier-Bresson, Robert Frank, and Garry Winogrand. The genre is distinct from documentary photography in its reactive and disinterested nature.

claims.text: Street photography is conducted for art or inquiry and features unmediated chance encounters and random incidents in public places.
claims.evidence_quote: Street photography is photography conducted for art or inquiry that features unmediated chance encounters and random incidents within public places.

claims.text: Street photography does not require a street or urban environment; it can depict objects or environments that project a human character.
claims.evidence_quote: Street photography does not necessitate the presence of a street or even the urban environment. Though people usually feature directly, street photography might be absent of people and can be of an object or environment where the image projects a decidedly human character in facsimile or aesthetic.

claims.text: The first photograph of figures in the street was taken by Louis Daguerre in 1838 or 1839.
claims.evidence_quote: In 1838 or 1839 the first photograph of figures in the street was recorded by Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre in one of a pair of daguerreotype views taken from his studio window of the Boulevard du Temple in Paris.

claims.text: Charles Nègre was the first photographer to achieve the technical sophistication to register people in movement on the street in Paris in 1851.
claims.evidence_quote: Charles Nègre was the first photographer to attain the technical sophistication required to register people in movement on the street in Paris in 1851.

claims.text: John Thomson published 'Street Life in London' in twelve monthly installments starting in February 1877.
claims.evidence_quote: Photographer John Thomson, a Scotsman working with journalist and social activist Adolphe Smith, published Street Life in London in twelve monthly installments starting in February 1877.

claims.text: The Leica, first sold in 1925, was the first commercially successful camera to use 35 mm film, enabling street photographers to capture fleeting moments.
claims.evidence_quote: First sold in 1925, the Leica was the first commercially successful camera to use 35 mm film. Its compactness and bright viewfinder, matched to lenses of quality (changeable on Leicas sold from 1930) helped photographers move through busy streets and capture fleeting moments.

claims.text: Henri Cartier-Bresson's book 'The Decisive Moment' promoted the idea of capturing a picture at the 'decisive moment'.
claims.evidence_quote: Henri Cartier-Bresson's widely admired Images à la Sauvette (1952) (the English-language edition was titled The Decisive Moment) promoted the idea of taking a picture at what he termed the 'decisive moment'; 'when form and content, vision and composition merged into a transcendent whole'.

claims.text: Robert Frank's 1958 book 'The Americans' challenged the formal rules of photography and is considered perhaps the most influential photography book of the 20th century.
claims.evidence_quote: Robert Frank's 1958 book, The Americans, was significant; raw and often out of focus, Frank's images questioned mainstream photography of the time, 'challenged all the formal rules laid down by Henri Cartier-Bresson and Walker Evans' and 'flew in the face of the wholesome pictorialism and heartfelt photojournalism of American magazines like LIFE and Time'.

claims.text: Garry Winogrand defined street photography as an attitude and style in the 1960s and 70s, and it has laboured in his shadow ever since.
claims.evidence_quote: In the 1960s and 70s, he defined street photography as an attitude as well as a style – and it has laboured in his shadow ever since, so definitive are his photographs of New York.

claims.text: Street photography is classically shot with wider angle lenses (e.g., 35mm) and usually features urban environments.
claims.evidence_quote: It is classically shot with wider angle lenses (e.g. 35mm) and usually features urban environments.

claims.text: Documentary photographers typically have a defined, premeditated message, while street photography is reactive and disinterested.
claims.evidence_quote: Documentary photographers typically have a defined, premeditated message and an intention to record particular events in history. Conversely, street photography is reactive and disinterested by nature and motivated by curiosity or creative inquiry.
